entities.name: Stephen Harding
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Stephen Harding, an English Benedictine monk who died on April 4, 1134, was instrumental in shaping one of the most influential monastic movements of the High Middle Ages: the Cistercian Order. As the third abbot of Cîteaux, he codified the foundational principles of Cistercian life, emphasizing a return to the strict observance of the Rule of Saint Benedict, austere living, manual labor, and liturgical simplicity. His leadership provided the institutional and spiritual framework that allowed the Cistercians to expand rapidly across Europe, profoundly impacting medieval spirituality, agriculture, architecture, and economics.

Harding's pivotal contribution was the drafting of the *Carta Caritatis* (Charter of Charity) between 1115 and 1119, which established the Cistercian system of federated monasteries under the authority of the Abbot of Cîteaux and the annual General Chapter. This innovative structure ensured uniformity of observance while granting daughter houses autonomy, a radical departure from the centralized Cluniac model. He also oversaw the meticulous revision of the Latin Vulgate Bible, known as the 'Bible of Stephen Harding,' completed around 1109, ensuring textual accuracy vital for monastic study and liturgy. His abbacy saw the exponential growth of Cîteaux, notably with the arrival of Bernard of Clairvaux and 30 companions in 1112, leading to the establishment of the first four daughter houses: La Ferté, Pontigny, Clairvaux, and Morimond.
